zh.title: 自己很喜欢，别人会买单吗？做产品最难跨过的这一步
zh.excerpt: 自己的需要可以让产品开始；真正走向市场，还要找到具体的问题、讲清价值，并完成一次真实交易。
zh.content:
“这个想法不错！”

“界面挺好看的。”

“加油，看好你。”

做产品的人，可能都想收下这些鼓励。但如果下一句是“那你愿意付费吗”，空气有时会突然安静。

从“挺好的”到“我买了”，中间到底隔着什么？

昨天，我写了三慢问道开始有付费记录的事。那个小小的开始让我开心，也让我想把这个问题继续往前想。

我愿意做自己喜欢的东西，也希望它能赚钱，能支持我继续做下去。

这两个愿望，值得放在同一张桌子上认真聊。

**从自己的需要出发，走向别人的生活。**

![自己很喜欢，别人会买单吗？把喜欢做成能长久的小生意。](/assets/notes/2026-10-02-will-others-pay/cover.png)

## 01｜自己是第一个用户，但别把自己当成整个市场

我做三慢问道，首先是因为自己想读。我每天读一章，尤其喜欢“对我们的启发”和“生活中的道”。这是一个真实的起点。

自己需要，有个好处：你知道麻烦在哪里，也容易发现哪里用着别扭。

但你愿意琢磨一小时的东西，别人可能只想花一分钟。你觉得有趣的细节，也可能正好挡住了别人最着急找的按钮。

于是，下一步要找的是：还有谁，在什么情况下，也会遇到这个麻烦？

可以先找几位符合这个场景的人聊聊。别急着介绍自己做了多少功能，先问三件事：

- 上一次遇到这个问题，是什么时候？
- 当时怎么解决，花了多少时间或钱？
- 现在的办法，哪里最让你不舒服？

比起“如果有个 App，你会不会用”，过去发生过的事，更值得听。

“有空试试”很客气。“我昨天就被这件事折腾了半天”，才让我们有东西可继续问。

## 02｜点赞很轻，换一种办法很重

假设你做了一个帮小商家整理商品图片的工具。

你介绍：“用了 AI，支持批量处理，还有好多风格。”

对方脑子里可能正在问：我的图能不能直接用？需要改几次？下周上新，还得重新折腾吗？

同一件产品，创作者在看功能，使用者在算自己能得到什么。

别人愿意买的价值，要落在他自己的生活里。

可能是少熬一次夜，少返工几轮；也可能是一段舒服的阅读、一张喜欢的照片，或者一个被认真照顾的时刻。价值不必都换算成“效率”。

可它需要具体到，让人能判断：这比我现在的办法，好在哪里？

对方已经有免费工具、旧习惯，甚至有“先不解决”的选项。你的产品，还要值得他花时间了解、学习和迁移。

这时我会试着写一句话：

> 我帮谁，在什么情况下，更轻松地完成什么；他为什么愿意为此付钱？

如果写着写着只剩下“强大”“智能”“全能”，我大概还得再想一会儿。

## 03｜先让一个小价值，完成一次真实交易

有时，没收到订单，我们的第一反应是加功能。

再加一个功能，再换一版首页，再让 AI 写三套介绍。忙得很踏实，那个“别人到底要不要”的问题，还原封不动地坐在那里。

我更想尝试的，是先拿出一个范围清楚、能够交付、价格明确的小版本。

比如前面那个图片工具，先让顾客买一次数量明确的图片处理服务，并把效果、修改范围和交付时间讲清楚。这里举的是验证方式，不是现成的赚钱案例。

有人买，认真问他为什么买；有人犹豫，也问清楚：是没看懂、不信任、价格不合适，还是这件事根本不着急？

免费试用能帮助发现使用问题。真实付款，会提供另一种信号。

当然，一笔订单也证明不了一门生意。接下来还要看交付是否满意，顾客会不会回来，或愿不愿意推荐给别人。

![喜欢怎样长成一门生意：自己需要、别人愿意买、长期做得下去。](/assets/notes/2026-10-02-will-others-pay/value-path.png)

**自己需要、别人愿意买、长期做得下去。**

## 04｜用户下个月，为什么还要给你钱？

我希望有持续收入。但“我希望每月收钱”，不是顾客每月付钱的理由。

收费方式，最好跟价值发生的方式对得上。

一次解锁、长期使用的内容，可以考虑买断，同时算清后续维护成本。

持续更新的内容、持续提供的服务，可以考虑订阅。要说清楚，订阅期间会不断得到什么。

使用量差异很大、每次使用又会产生明显成本的服务，可以考虑按次或按额度收费。

收款方式可以不同，问题始终是：这笔钱，对方觉得值吗？

订阅产品尤其要回答续费的理由。用户又不是给我们发生活费。

他第一次为好奇心付钱，第二次还愿意留下，往往需要我们继续把承诺的价值交到他手里。

## 05｜收到了钱，还要留得住利润和生活

商业化还有两道不太浪漫、但绕不过去的题。

第一道：下一个顾客从哪里来？

第一批人可能因为认识你而购买。再往后，能不能通过搜索、内容、推荐或合作，稳定地遇到真正有需求的人？这些方式都需要投入，写内容也会花时间。

第二道：每多一笔订单，究竟剩下什么？

平台和支付费用、AI 调用、服务器、获客、退款、售后，都得记下来。钱之外，也要记自己的工时。

假设一个订单收 100 元，相关变动成本是 30 元，先剩下 70 元。可这还没扣固定支出、税费，也没给自己投入的时间计价。

如果每一单都要手忙脚乱地陪两个小时，就得继续看：价格、交付范围和流程，哪一处需要调整？

这是个假设算例，但提醒很真实：收入增加的时候，也要看看自己是不是越来越累。

我想慢慢找到的，是这样一种状态：有人需要，愿意购买；我能稳定交付，扣除成本之后有余量，也还有力气继续创造。

这才是我愿意长期经营的小生意。

## 06｜一休、不二、三慢：生意想走远，人也要被照顾

认真讨论赚钱，是因为作品需要持续投入，生活也有账单。

但我也不想把自己的每一天，都变成一张等待上涨的报表。

一个产品卖得不好，需要调整的是定位、价格或体验。它不该轻易变成“我这个人不行”的证据。

这也是我想放在工作和生活里的人生观：

**一休：先照顾身体，安顿情绪，再继续前行。**

累的时候允许自己停一停。有些决定，睡好一觉再做，可能比硬撑到凌晨更清楚。

**不二：不评判，没有好坏对错，接纳高峰与低谷，拥抱完整而非完美。**

放在这里，是提醒自己：认真判断产品和经营，也不急着用一时的结果，给自己或别人贴上成败的标签。

**三慢：慢下来，慢慢来，慢慢成为。**

把眼前一件事做好，听一次真实反馈，完成一次可靠交付。让生意一点点长出自己的节奏。

**如水：向内扎根，向外流动；顺应变化，不失本心。**

愿意听市场的声音，也记得自己为什么开始。

慢慢做，也好好活。

我们愿陪伴彼此走过低谷与高峰，探索身心健康的工作与生活方式；真实面对自己与世界，善待自己、他人与生命，并在创造和欣赏中活出生命之美。

![一休、不二、三慢、如水：慢慢做，也好好活。](/assets/notes/2026-10-02-will-others-pay/work-and-life.png)

从“我喜欢做”，慢慢走到“有人需要、愿意买，我也能长期做下去”。

把喜欢做成生意，也把日子过成自己愿意继续的样子。

**#一休不二三慢**

配图取意于虾子曰艺术风格图鉴推荐的 **Anime／日漫风格**。用一间温暖的街角小店，画出创造、交换与生活的关系，也是一次审美与表达的练习。

en.label: Field Notes
en.title: You Love It. Will Anyone Pay for It? The Hardest Step in Building a Product
en.excerpt: Your own need can start a product. Reaching a market takes a concrete problem, clear value, a small real transaction, and a business you can keep running.
en.content:
“That’s a good idea.”

“The interface looks great.”

“Keep going. I believe in you.”

Anyone who makes products is happy to hear encouragement like this. But if the next question is, “Would you pay for it?” the room can suddenly become very quiet.

What lies between “That’s nice” and “I bought it”?

Yesterday I wrote about Wendao recording its first paid transactions. That small beginning made me happy, and it also made me want to carry this question a little further.

I want to make things I care about. I also want them to earn money so I can keep making them.

Those two wishes deserve to sit at the same table.

**Begin with a need of your own, then move into someone else’s life.**

![You love it. Will anyone pay for it? Turning something you care about into a small business that can last. The original artwork contains Chinese text.](/assets/notes/2026-10-02-will-others-pay/cover.png)

## 01｜Be Your First User, but Do Not Mistake Yourself for the Whole Market

I began making Wendao because I wanted to read it myself. I read one chapter a day, and I especially enjoy the sections about what the text can teach us and how the Tao appears in daily life. That is a real starting point.

Building for a need you understand has an advantage: you know where the frustration lives, and you can quickly notice where the experience feels awkward.

But something you are willing to explore for an hour may get only one minute from someone else. A detail you find delightful may sit directly in front of the button they urgently need.

So the next question is: who else encounters this problem, and in what situation?

Start by talking with a few people who actually live in that situation. Do not rush to explain how many features you have built. Ask three things first:

- When did this problem last happen?
- What did you do then, and how much time or money did it cost?
- What is most frustrating about the way you handle it today?

Past behavior is more useful than asking, “If there were an app for this, would you use it?”

“I’ll try it sometime” is polite. “This wasted half my day yesterday” gives you something real to investigate.

## 02｜A Like Is Light; Changing How You Work Is Heavy

Imagine that you made a tool to help small shops organize product images.

You introduce it by saying, “It uses AI, processes images in batches, and offers lots of styles.”

The shop owner may be asking very different questions: Can I use the results as they are? How many rounds of revision will this take? When I launch next week’s products, will I have to do everything again?

The maker sees features. The user is calculating what will change in their own life.

Value that someone will pay for has to land in that person’s world.

It might mean one fewer late night or several fewer rounds of rework. It could also mean an enjoyable reading experience, a photograph they love, or a moment in which they feel carefully looked after. Value does not always have to be translated into efficiency.

It does have to be concrete enough for someone to judge: how is this better than what I already do?

They already have free tools, familiar habits, and even the option of leaving the problem unsolved. Your product has to be worth the time needed to understand it, learn it, and move over to it.

At this point, I try to write one sentence:

> Who do I help, in what situation, to accomplish what more easily—and why would they pay for that?

If the sentence collapses into words like “powerful,” “intelligent,” and “all-in-one,” I probably need to think a little longer.

## 03｜Let One Small Piece of Value Complete One Real Transaction

When no orders arrive, our first reaction is often to add features.

We add another function, redesign the homepage, and ask AI for three new versions of the copy. We stay reassuringly busy while the original question—does anyone actually want this?—remains exactly where it was.

I would rather begin with a small version whose scope is clear, whose outcome can be delivered, and whose price is visible.

For the image tool above, that might mean selling a service for a defined number of product images, with the expected result, revision limits, and delivery time stated clearly. This is an example of a validation method, not a ready-made success story.

If someone buys, ask carefully why. If someone hesitates, find out what stopped them. Did they fail to understand it? Do they not trust the result? Is the price wrong? Or is the problem simply not urgent?

A free trial can reveal usability problems. A real payment supplies a different kind of signal.

One order, of course, does not prove a business. You still have to learn whether the customer is satisfied, returns, or recommends you to someone else.

![How something you love can grow into a business: you need it, other people will pay for it, and you can keep doing it over time. The original artwork contains Chinese text.](/assets/notes/2026-10-02-will-others-pay/value-path.png)

**You need it. Other people will pay for it. You can keep doing it over time.**

## 04｜Why Should the Customer Pay You Again Next Month?

I want recurring revenue. But “I want to collect money every month” is not a reason for a customer to pay every month.

The way you charge should match the way value appears.

For content that is unlocked once and used for a long time, a one-time purchase may make sense—as long as future maintenance costs are included in the decision.

For continuously updated content or an ongoing service, a subscription may fit. You need to say clearly what continues to arrive during the subscription.

For a service with very different usage levels and a meaningful cost each time it is used, charging per use or by credits may be more appropriate.

The payment model can change. The central question does not: does the customer believe this is worth the money?

Subscriptions in particular need a reason to renew. The user is not paying us a monthly allowance.

Curiosity may win the first payment. For the customer to stay, we usually have to keep placing the promised value in their hands.

## 05｜After Money Arrives, You Still Need to Keep Profit—and a Life

Commercializing a product brings two more questions. They are not romantic, but there is no way around them.

The first is: where does the next customer come from?

The first few people may buy because they know you. After that, can search, content, referrals, or partnerships help you meet people who truly have the need? Every channel requires an investment. Writing content costs time too.

The second is: what remains after each additional order?

Platform and payment fees, AI usage, servers, customer acquisition, refunds, and support all have to be recorded. Your own working hours belong in the calculation as well.

Suppose an order brings in CNY 100 and its variable costs total CNY 30. That leaves CNY 70 at first. But fixed expenses and taxes have not been deducted, and your time has not been priced.

If every order sends you scrambling for two hours, you need to look again at the price, delivery scope, and process. Which part needs to change?

The numbers are hypothetical, but the reminder is real: when revenue grows, check whether your exhaustion is growing too.

I want to move gradually toward a state in which people need what I make and are willing to buy it; I can deliver reliably, retain a margin after costs, and still have energy left to create.

That is the kind of small business I am willing to run for a long time.

## 06｜Rest, Wholeness, Slowness: If the Business Is to Last, the Person Needs Care Too

I take earning money seriously because a body of work needs continued investment, and life comes with bills.

But I do not want to turn every day into a chart waiting to go up.

If a product sells poorly, perhaps its positioning, price, or experience needs work. That result should not easily become evidence that “I am a failure.”

This is also the philosophy I want to carry into work and life:

**Yixiu—rest first: care for the body, settle the emotions, then continue.**

When you are tired, allow yourself to pause. Some decisions become clearer after a good night’s sleep than after forcing yourself to work until dawn.

**Buer—do not divide life into simple judgments: receive peaks and valleys, and embrace wholeness instead of perfection.**

Here it reminds me to judge a product and its business honestly without rushing to label myself or anyone else a success or failure because of one temporary result.

**Sanman—slow down, go gradually, and become over time.**

Do the next piece of work well. Listen to one piece of honest feedback. Complete one dependable delivery. Let the business grow into its own rhythm.

**Like water—take root within and flow outward; adapt to change without losing what matters.**

Listen to the market, and remember why you began.

Build slowly. Live well too.

We want to accompany one another through valleys and peaks, exploring healthier ways to work and live; to face ourselves and the world honestly, treat ourselves, other people, and life with care, and discover beauty through creating and appreciating.

![Yixiu, Buer, Sanman, and water: build slowly, and live well too. The original artwork contains Chinese text.](/assets/notes/2026-10-02-will-others-pay/work-and-life.png)

Move gradually from “I love making this” to “people need it, will pay for it, and I can keep doing it.”

Turn what you love into a business, and shape your days into a life you still want to continue.

**#RestWholenessSlowness**

The illustrations draw on the **Anime style** recommended by Xiazi Style Atlas. A warm corner shop becomes a way to picture the relationship among creation, exchange, and daily life—and another exercise in visual taste and expression.
